# Equality in depth Brunn--Minkowski and strict inclusion monotonicity

For a full-dimensional convex body \(K\subset\mathbb R^d\), \(d\ge1\), let
\[
 A(K)=\max_{g\in K}\min_{u\in S^{d-1}}
              |K\cap\{x:u\cdot(x-g)\ge0\}|.
\]
The maximum is attained, is positive, and every maximizing point is interior. These elementary facts, and
\[
 A(sK+tL)^{1/d}\ge sA(K)^{1/d}+tA(L)^{1/d}
                 \qquad(s,t\ge0),                       \tag{1}
\]
were proved in continuous-depth-brunn-minkowski.md.

For positive \(s,t\), equality in (1) holds **if and only if \(K\) and \(L\) are positively homothetic**. The conclusion concerns the entire bodies. Equality of one pair of active caps alone would not suffice; the proof uses both the centroids of their boundary sections and a covering collection of active directions.

More precisely, if \(g_K,g_L\) are any chosen ordinary deepest points and equality holds, put
\[
                  r=\left(\frac{A(L)}{A(K)}\right)^{1/d}.
\]
Then
\[
                         L=r(K-g_K)+g_L.                 \tag{2}
\]
No strict convexity or smooth boundary is assumed.

## 1. The section centroid of an active directional cap

For an interior point \(g\), write
\[
 \phi_K(u,g)=|K\cap\{x:u\cdot(x-g)\ge0\}|,\qquad |u|=1.
\]
Every through-\(g\) section is a full \((d-1)\)-dimensional convex body in its plane. If \(u\) minimizes \(\phi_K(\cdot,g)\), then
\[
       \frac{\displaystyle\int_{K\cap\{u\cdot(x-g)=0\}}
                          x\,dH_{d-1}(x)}
            {\displaystyle H_{d-1}
                      (K\cap\{u\cdot(x-g)=0\})}=g.       \tag{3}
\]

For \(d=1\), the section is the singleton \(\{g\}\), and (3) is immediate with \(H_0=1\). For \(d\ge2\), translate \(g\) to zero and rotate \(u\) to the last coordinate direction. Write \(x=(y,z)\). For \(v\perp u\), changing the normal to \(u+\tau v\) changes the inequality to
\[
                         z\ge-\tau v\cdot y.
\]
Fubini and dominated convergence give
\[
 \left.\frac{d}{d\tau}\right|_{\tau=0}
   |K\cap\{(u+\tau v)\cdot(x-g)\ge0\}|
       =\int_{K\cap\{u\cdot(x-g)=0\}}v\cdot(x-g)\,dH_{d-1}(x).
                                                               \tag{4}
\]
Here is a direct justification at nonsmooth bodies. For each fixed \(y\), the vertical slice of \(K\) is a closed interval, possibly empty. Except on the boundary of the proper section, which has \((d-1)\)-measure zero, its length derivative at threshold zero is \(v\cdot y\) if \((y,0)\) is in that section and zero otherwise. A relative interior point of a section whose plane meets \(\operatorname{int}K\) belongs to \(\operatorname{int}K\), so neither slice endpoint is zero there. The difference quotient is bounded by \(|v\cdot y|\), on a bounded projection of \(K\). This proves (4).

Positive normalization of \(u+\tau v\) does not change its cap. At a minimizing normal the derivative (4) vanishes for every tangent vector \(v\). The vector integral of \(x-g\) itself lies in \(u^\perp\), so it must vanish. This proves (3).

In particular (3) holds for every active cap at an ordinary deepest point. It is a statement about the section centroid, not an assertion that the deepest point is the centroid of the whole body.

## 2. Active normals at a deepest point cover all directions

Let \(g\) be an ordinary deepest point of \(K\), and define the compact nonempty active-normal set
\[
                U=\{u\in S^{d-1}:\phi_K(u,g)=A(K)\}.
\]
Then
\[
                              0\in\operatorname{conv}U. \tag{5}
\]

For completeness, suppose otherwise. Strict separation supplies a vector \(v\) and \(c>0\) with \(u\cdot v\ge c\) for every \(u\in U\). Choose an open neighborhood \(O\) of \(U\) in the sphere where \(u\cdot v\ge c/2\). An interior ball \(B(g,r_0)\subset K\) supplies a uniform positive lower bound on all section areas at distances at most \(r_0/2\) from \(g\). Moving \(g\) a small distance in direction \(-v\) therefore increases every cap with normal in \(O\) by a uniform positive multiple of that distance.

On the compact complement of \(O\), the original cap masses exceed \(A(K)\) by a uniform positive gap. A bounded containing ball supplies a uniform slab upper bound, so a sufficiently small center movement keeps all of those cap masses strictly above \(A(K)\) as well. The moved point remains interior. Its minimum cap mass is therefore larger than \(A(K)\), a contradiction. This argument handles \(d=1\) by the interval section convention as well.

Carathéodory gives finitely many \(u_1,\ldots,u_\ell\in U\), \(\ell\le d+1\), and positive weights summing to one with
\[
                           \sum_i\alpha_i u_i=0.
\]
Their closed through-\(g\) halfspaces cover \(\mathbb R^d\):
\[
                    \bigcup_i\{x:u_i\cdot(x-g)\ge0\}
                                      =\mathbb R^d.     \tag{6}
\]
Indeed a point strictly outside them all would make the weighted sum of its margins strictly negative. No assumption that the active normals span full rank is needed for this closed covering fact.

## 3. Equality propagates from caps to both entire bodies

Let \(g_K,g_L\) attain the respective ordinary maxima and put
\[
 M=sK+tL,\qquad g=sg_K+tg_L,\qquad
 a=\bigl(sA(K)^{1/d}+tA(L)^{1/d}\bigr)^d.
\]
The point \(g\) is interior to \(M\). The proof of (1) gives
\[
                             \phi_M(u,g)\ge a
                           \qquad\text{for every }u.   \tag{7}
\]
Assume equality \(A(M)=a\). Then \(g\) is a deepest point of \(M\). Choose active normals \(u_1,\ldots,u_\ell\) covering \(\mathbb R^d\) as in Section 2.

For any one of these normals, write
\[
 K_i=K\cap\{u_i\cdot(x-g_K)\ge0\},\qquad
 L_i=L\cap\{u_i\cdot(x-g_L)\ge0\}.
\]
All terms in the following chain are equal:
\[
 \begin{split}
 a^{1/d}
 &=\phi_M(u_i,g)^{1/d}\\
 &\ge |sK_i+tL_i|^{1/d}\\
 &\ge s|K_i|^{1/d}+t|L_i|^{1/d}\\
 &\ge sA(K)^{1/d}+tA(L)^{1/d}=a^{1/d}.                \tag{8}
 \end{split}
\]
Because \(s,t>0\), the last equality forces \(|K_i|=A(K)\) and \(|L_i|=A(L)\) individually. These are active caps at their own deepest points. Their volumes are positive.

Classical equality in Brunn--Minkowski for full-dimensional convex bodies now gives
\[
                         L_i=rK_i+b_i,\qquad
                      r=(A(L)/A(K))^{1/d}>0.            \tag{9}
\]
The ratio is the same for every \(i\). It remains essential to prove that the translations are also the same.

The exposed face of \(K_i\) minimizing the functional \(u_i\cdot x\) is exactly
\[
                  K\cap\{u_i\cdot(x-g_K)=0\};
\]
the analogous minimum face of \(L_i\) is its through-\(g_L\) section. These are proper full \((d-1)\)-sections. Positive homothety (9) maps one face to the other. By (3), their centroids are \(g_K\) and \(g_L\). Affine covariance of the section centroid therefore implies
\[
                            b_i=g_L-rg_K                \tag{10}
\]
for every active \(i\).

Let \(\mathcal H(x)=r(x-g_K)+g_L\). Equations (9)--(10) show \(\mathcal H(K_i)=L_i\) for every selected normal. The same normals also give covering through-center halfspaces at \(g_K\) and \(g_L\), because their positive balance is independent of the center. Thus
\[
 K=\bigcup_i K_i,\qquad L=\bigcup_i L_i,
 \qquad \mathcal H(K)=\bigcup_i\mathcal H(K_i)=L.         \tag{11}
\]
This proves (2), and is the step that rules out unrelated changes in the uncaptured parts of the bodies.

Conversely, if \(L=rK+b\), then
\[
 sK+tL=(s+tr)K+tb,\qquad A(L)=r^dA(K),
\]
so equality in (1) follows from translation invariance and scaling of \(A\).

The equality chain also shows that every selected active cap of \(M\) is the exact Minkowski sum of the corresponding endpoint caps: the inclusion has equal positive volumes, so equality of the convex sets follows. That stronger cap statement is consistent with, but not needed after, the whole-body conclusion (11).

## 4. Strict monotonicity for every proper inclusion

If \(K\subset L\) are full-dimensional convex bodies and \(K\ne L\), then
\[
                              A(K)<A(L).                \tag{12}
\]
Ordinary depth is monotone under inclusion. If equality held, then
\[
                  K\subset(K+L)/2\subset L
\]
would force \(A((K+L)/2)=A(K)=A(L)\). Equality in (1) would give \(L=K+b\), since their \(A\)-values force the homothety ratio to be one. The bodies would have equal volume. Proper inclusion of full-dimensional compact convex bodies strictly increases volume, so \(K=L\), a contradiction.

This strengthens the earlier strict-interior-containment statement. It does not supply a uniform numerical gap for a sequence approaching equality.

## 5. Strict ordinary quasiconcavity and uniqueness

For a fixed body put
\[
                     f_K(g)=\min_u\phi_K(u,g).
\]
This ordinary pointwise depth is strictly quasiconcave on \(\operatorname{int}K\): if \(g_0\ne g_1\) are interior and \(0<t<1\), then
\[
 f_K((1-t)g_0+tg_1)>
                       \min\{f_K(g_0),f_K(g_1)\}.       \tag{12a}
\]

First ordinary quasiconcavity follows directly because a cap threshold at the interpolated point lies between the two endpoint thresholds. Equivalently, the cap-set Minkowski inclusion proves the stronger concavity of \(f_K^{1/d}\).

Suppose equality with the positive value \(a=\min\{f_K(g_0),f_K(g_1)\}\) held in (12a), and choose an attaining normal \(u\) at the intermediate point. If \(u\cdot g_0\ne u\cdot g_1\), the endpoint with the larger threshold has strictly smaller cap mass than the intermediate point. The strictness follows by integrating the positive section areas between two proper interior levels of a full-dimensional convex body. Its cap mass would be less than \(a\), contradicting that endpoint's depth.

Thus \(u\cdot g_0=u\cdot g_1\), so the same hyperplane cuts both endpoints and its cap has mass \(a\). It is active at both endpoints, whose depths must then both equal \(a\). Section 1 says that the centroid of this one fixed section is both \(g_0\) and \(g_1\), a contradiction. This proof covers unequal endpoint depths as well: the common cap of mass \(a\) would already contradict the larger depth.

For every \(0<a<A(K)\), the ordinary depth region
\[
                         \{g\in K:f_K(g)\ge a\}
\]
is a full-dimensional strictly convex compact set. Positivity keeps it inside \(\operatorname{int}K\); continuity and (12a) place each open segment between distinct points in the interior of the region. In particular the deepest point is unique.

Uniqueness also follows from the center-aligned equality theorem: applying (2) to \(L=K\) and any two deepest points gives \(K=K+(g_1-g_0)\), impossible for a bounded nonempty body unless the centers agree.

These statements are explicitly **ordinary continuous** depth statements. Summed mixed-fiber cap functions can have supporting-facet contributions and do not inherit this section-centroid argument automatically.

## 6. Exact equality at a compatible midpoint

Suppose full-dimensional convex bodies satisfy
\[
          (K_0+K_2)/2\subset K_1,\qquad
 A(K_1)^{1/d}=\frac{A(K_0)^{1/d}+A(K_2)^{1/d}}2.       \tag{13}
\]
Monotonicity and (1) force equality of \(A(K_1)\) with \(A((K_0+K_2)/2)\). Strict inclusion monotonicity (12) then gives
\[
                         K_1=(K_0+K_2)/2.
\]
Equality in (1) also makes \(K_0,K_2\) homothetic, with ratio determined by their \(A\)-values. Their unique deepest points obey the corresponding homothety and midpoint identities.

Thus zero depth-root slack at an actual midpoint forces a whole-body equality model. It does not imply full Jensen affinity from merely the relations of a prescribed forest. The existing zero-slack homothetic forest counterexample remains pertinent to that separate inference.

All statements here concern positive full-dimensional bodies and positive coefficients for the equality classification. A zero coefficient in (1) makes equality automatic and supplies no rigidity. No extension to changing intrinsic direction spaces, nor a mixed-integer depth conclusion, is asserted.
